notes.body:
Free will (إرادة) is a structural feature built into the creature — **it is the machinery by which a person can choose.** Divine forsakenness (خذلان) is something else: the moment when Allah, in His infinite completeness, steps back and allows the creature to proceed unsupported by His divine aid.

True magnificence (جلال) is self-sufficient. A glory that could only sustain itself by compelling admiration would be fragile — not truly magnificent at all. The sun does not dim because someone closes their eyes to it. **Allah's magnificence remains entirely undiminished by those who turn from Him** — which is precisely why His greatness is the ground on which disobedience becomes possible: an infinite grandeur has no need to compel.

Free will explains how a creature can choose; magnificence explains why the choice was left open. If worship were compelled, it would not be worship (عبادة) — that love-laden, freely given devotion. A bow made under duress is performance, and **performance was never what Allah asked of us.**

خذلان, then, is not a failure of divine love — **it is the shadow that real love casts.** When a father steps back and lets his child walk without holding his hand, it is the fullness of his trust, not its absence, that makes the stepping-back possible. Allah's magnificence is so encompassing that it can allow the creature to stumble. Free will is the door; خذلان is what happens when the Creator, in the vastness of His greatness, chooses not to hold it shut.

etymology: خذلان (divine forsakenness): from the root خ-ذ-ل, meaning to withdraw support and leave one stranded. خذل originally described a companion who abandons his fellow mid-battle. Its verbal noun, خذلان, names the state of being left without divine aid — the creature carried forward only by its own limited momentum.

جلال (magnificence): from the root ج-ل-ل, meaning to be immeasurably great or majestic. The root captures something so vast it overwhelms the gaze. Paired with جمال (beauty), جلال names the awe-inducing face of the divine — a greatness before which even the faculty of understanding falls short.

إرادة (will, intention): from the root ر-و-د, meaning to seek or move purposefully toward something. The root pictures a deliberate going-toward. إرادة is the faculty of directed intention — the inner reach toward a chosen end. In the creature it is derived and dependent; in Allah it is absolute.

notes.body:
The passage uses خذلان to name something very specific: **Allah's own act of withdrawing His divine support** from a creature — not the creature's disobedience itself, and not some neutral capacity sitting passively inside us waiting to tip either way.

Think of it this way. Allah's support — His grace, His توفيق — is like a hand steadying a candle in the wind. When that hand is present, the flame holds. When Allah withdraws that steadying hand, the wind of temptation can extinguish it. خذلان is the withdrawal of the hand, not the wind, and not the darkness that follows.

This is why the passage says Allah allows disobedience through خذلان but is **not content with it**. He permits it — His magnificence is so vast that it contains even the possibility of turning away from Him — but He does not desire it. A king powerful enough to imprison every rebel may still choose not to, yet his heart is not at peace with the rebellion.

Disobedience is not described as a crime first — it is described as a *contradiction*. If عبادة is a lover's obedience, then خذلان is the moment the lover stops listening, not because the beloved became unworthy, but because the divine support that kept the heart attentive was graciously withdrawn. The creature was given room, and in that room, it failed.

Allah did not create us for that failure:

وَمَا خَلَقْتُ ٱلْجِنَّ وَٱلْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ
And I created not the jinns and humans except that they should worship Me.
Al-Dhariyat 51:56

خذلان is therefore the shadow side of our freedom — the proof that **our obedience is chosen, not compelled**. A love that cannot be refused is not love at all; it is mechanism.

etymology: خذلان (divine abandonment): from the root خ-ذ-ل, to leave someone without help precisely when they need it. خاذل is the one who abandons; خذلان is the act of withdrawal itself. Its opposite is توفيق — divine assistance. The root carries the sting of a companion who turns away at the critical moment, making خذلان not indifference but a deliberate, purposeful withholding.
